lines.text: A land bridge between Europe and Asia, where the first temples rose and empires met. This is the story of Turkey, from Gobekli Tepe to today.
Nearly twelve thousand years ago, hunter-gatherers raised rings of carved stone pillars on a hilltop, among the oldest great monuments on Earth.
A few thousand years later, farmers at Catalhoyuk packed their mud-brick houses together and climbed in through the roofs.
On the north-west coast rose Troy, layer upon layer of city, remembered forever as the setting of Homer's Trojan War.
On the central plateau the Hittites built an empire, fought Egypt at Kadesh, and signed one of the oldest peace treaties we know.
On the western coast, Greek settlers founded Ephesus, a city that would flourish for centuries under Greeks and then Romans.
There they raised the vast marble Temple of Artemis, one of the wonders of the ancient world.
Further south, at today's Bodrum, a grand tomb was built for the ruler Mausolus, and gave us the word mausoleum.
In 330 the emperor Constantine refounded old Byzantium on the Bosphorus as Constantinople, a city on two continents and capital of an empire.
Its mighty triple land walls went up in the fifth century and held off attackers for a thousand years.
In 537 Justinian's great domed church, Hagia Sophia, was finished, the wonder of the Byzantine world.
Far to the east, Turkish rulers called the Seljuks were building an empire of their own, and looking west.
In 1071 at Manzikert, the Seljuks defeated and captured the Byzantine emperor, and Anatolia was opened to the Turks.
In Konya, the Persian poet Rumi settled and wrote of love and the search for God, verses still read the world over.
Around 1299 a small Turkish state was founded in Anatolia. The Ottoman Empire would last more than six hundred years.
In 1432 a prince was born who would be called the Conqueror. Sultan Mehmed the second had his eyes on Constantinople.
In 1453, after a siege of about two months, his cannon broke the walls, and the Byzantine Empire came to an end.
On the hill above the city, the sultans built Topkapi Palace, their home and seat of power for about four centuries.
Mimar Sinan, chief architect for some fifty years, filled the empire with hundreds of mosques, bridges and schools.
Under Suleiman the Magnificent the empire reached its height, taking Belgrade and Rhodes and besieging Vienna, while he reformed its laws.
In 1616 the Blue Mosque was completed, with its six minarets and Iznik tiles, facing Hagia Sophia across the square.
By the nineteenth century the empire was in decline. In 1881 a boy was born in Salonica who would become Ataturk.
In the First World War, Allied forces landed at Gallipoli to seize the straits. After months of fighting they withdrew.
But the war was lost, and the land was occupied. Mustafa Kemal led the fight against partition and won.
In 1923 the Treaty of Lausanne drew the borders of modern Turkey, with a vast exchange of people between Greece and Turkey.
That year Ankara, in the heart of Anatolia, was made the new capital.
And the Republic of Turkey was declared, rising from the ruins of the Ottoman Empire, with Ataturk as its first president.
In 1928 Turkish switched from Arabic script to a new Latin alphabet, almost overnight.
In 1934 Turkish women won the vote in national elections, ahead of many countries in Europe.
In 1952 Orhan Pamuk was born in Istanbul, the novelist who would win Turkey's first Nobel Prize in Literature.
Two years later came Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who would lead the country from 2003, first as prime minister and then as president.
In 1980 the army seized power, one of several times the military stepped into Turkish politics.
In August 1999 an earthquake near Izmit killed some seventeen thousand people in the country's north-west.
In 2016 part of the army tried to overthrow the government, and the attempt was defeated within a single night.
Then in February 2023, two huge earthquakes struck the south near Syria, killing tens of thousands and flattening whole towns.
Temples, empires and a young republic, all on one land where two continents meet.
